quotes.quote: “It is in itself a very serious matter that the Ukrainian side violated the confidentiality agreement between the two countries and made the disclosure unilaterally,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said Sunday night.

“But the Ukrainian presidential press office’s false statement that there had been no confidentiality agreement, seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries.”
The presidential secretary further stated that the South Korean government is “considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter,” without further explanation.
The Ukrainian ambassador to South Korea was summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday as Seoul demands an official apology and an explanation of how this happened.

“From the perspective of those who advertised the repatriation to the whole world with enthusiastic fanfare to show off their achievements – regardless of the impact on inter-Korean relations, the loss of life, or the damage to national interests – they likely not only cannot understand our government’s efforts to keep it confidential but may even wonder if there is something wrong with it,” Lee wrote just hours after Zelensky’s address in New York.
“I do not know the reasons behind Ukraine’s disclosure in violation of the non-disclosure agreement, but it is deeply regrettable.”

James Kim, director of the Korea Program at the Stimson Center, told the Washington Examiner that Zelensky’s disclosure has put Lee and his government in a terrible situation that will likely force them to compromise their campaign to normalize relations with the North or face domestic backlash.

“The current administration in Seoul wants to re-engage with North Korea, and taking on prisoners of war from Ukraine would complicate that plan because North Korea would see that as an act that is in concert with their adversary,” Kim said.
Kim Jong Un’s regime has not publicly commented on the situation yet, but if it does, a demand for repatriation will be further complicated by the two detainees’ request for asylum in South Korea.
Both have expressed a desire to integrate into the southern half of the peninsula and live normal lives.

“[Repatriating the prisoners] can potentially be looked upon as a violation of human rights because they know that the North Korean government is not very tolerant of anyone that decides to defect or has expressed the desire to do so.
And so returning them would effectively mean that they would either be tortured or they would be imprisoned for life or even put to death,” Kim explained.
